node-1.label: Patient experienced recurrent arrhythmia during hospitalization, notably in left lateral decubitus position with palpitations

node-2.label: Patient is in their 30s, has obesity, and a history of alcohol use

node-3.label: Hospital course was complicated by delirium tremens, intubation, and ventilator-associated pneumonia requiring multiple courses of antibiotics; two weeks prior, PICC insertion and tracheostomy had been performed

node-4.label: Arrhythmia episodes were associated with palpitations, without chest pain, dyspnea, presyncope, or hemodynamic compromise

node-5.label: Two-dimensional echocardiography showed normal left ventricular function without structural abnormalities

why.why: Alcohol use, delirium tremens and normal cardiac structure still support withdrawal-related arrhythmia, but new chest radiography shows PICC tip displacement into the right atrium at tricuspid valve level, which the radiologist interprets as more strongly supporting PICC-induced arrhythmia. The laboratory expert also notes that ECG, electrolytes, CIWA-Ar and Holter results are unavailable, so the temporal relationship between alcohol withdrawal and arrhythmia cannot be confirmed. Therefore confidence is reduced from 0.35 to 0.25.

Recent PICC insertion and left-lateral positional symptoms already suggested catheter-related arrhythmia. New cardiac monitoring shows fusion beat and PVC morphology matching the clinical arrhythmia, and chest radiography confirms PICC tip displacement into the right atrium at tricuspid valve level, providing a direct mechanical explanation for positional ectopy. The radiologist explicitly favors PICC-induced arrhythmia over alcohol withdrawal. Confidence is increased from 0.30 to 0.55.

Multiple antibiotic courses remain a possible trigger, but new imaging evidence provides a more compelling mechanical cause (PICC tip at tricuspid valve level), and neither expert analysis supports antibiotic-induced arrhythmia. The hypothesis is therefore less likely, decreasing confidence from 0.20 to 0.10.

Obesity and benign positional palpitations remain, but the newly confirmed PICC tip displacement offers a stronger explanation for the positional arrhythmia, and there is no new supportive evidence for obesity-related ectopy. Confidence is reduced from 0.15 to 0.10.
